lead: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad goal of making machines do tasks that need intelligence. Machine learning (ML) is one way to reach it: the program improves from examples instead of following rules typed by a person. Deep learning (DL) is ML with many stacked layers, so the network learns its own features. The three form nested circles. This chapter gives a one-line test for each circle, then a short dated history from the 1943 neuron to today's large models. You use these labels whenever you read a product claim or choose a model for a task.
prereq: You need: school-level algebra, where a function maps an input to an output; no earlier chapter is required.

blocks.text: AI is the outer circle. A system is AI if it does a task that would need intelligence from a person: play chess, prove a theorem, answer a question. The rules may be written by hand. A chess engine that checks legal moves and uses a hand-written search is AI, but it does not learn from data.

ML is the next circle. A system is ML if its rules come from data. You show it input-output pairs, or just inputs, and an algorithm adjusts numbers inside the model so its output gets closer to what you want. House-price prediction from past sales is ML. k-means grouping customers by spend is ML.

DL is the inner circle. A system is DL if it is ML and its model has many layers stacked one after another. Each layer changes the numbers passing through it. Early layers learn simple features; later layers combine them into complex features. Face recognition from pixels with 8 layers is DL. A single straight-line fit is not DL, even if it learns from data.

items: AI: does a machine do a task that needs intelligence, even with hand-written rules?
ML: does the program improve from data instead of being told every rule?
DL: is it ML with many stacked layers that learn their own features?

blocks.text: The tests are nested. Every DL system is ML and AI. Some AI systems are not ML. Many ML systems are not DL.
The history is a line of ideas, not a smooth climb. Each step added a piece that later models used. Some syllabi call this the history and evolution of neural networks.

items: 1943: McCulloch and Pitts wrote a neuron as a weighted sum followed by a threshold. It could compute AND, OR and NOT; it could not learn.
1958: Rosenblatt's perceptron learned weights from examples by changing them after mistakes.
1969: Minsky and Papert showed a single perceptron cannot solve XOR. The limit was real for one layer; it slowed neural-network funding.
1986: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams made backpropagation practical for multilayer networks. Hidden layers could now get useful weight updates.
2012: AlexNet, a deep CNN, won ImageNet with a large error drop. Graphics cards and a big labelled dataset made deep networks practical.
After 2012: deeper CNNs, recurrent models and then transformers scaled to large text and image models.

blocks.text: Three model families appear in this line. A CNN uses local filters over a grid such as an image (see Unit 3, Convolutional Neural Networks). An RNN reads a sequence one step at a time and keeps a state (see Unit 4, Recurrent Networks and Sequence Models). A transformer uses attention to compare all positions in a sequence (see Unit 5, Attention, Transformers and Language Models). The 1943 formula is in Chapter 1.4; the learned version is in Chapter 1.5.

sections.h3: Why deep learning needed data and compute

blocks.text: In older ML, a person designs the features. For a loan model, a person decides that income, existing debt and repayment history matter, then gives those columns to a classifier. The model learns weights for those columns, not the columns themselves.

Deep learning shifts that work into the network. The first layers of an image network learn edges; later layers learn shapes; the last layers learn faces. Nobody writes the edge detector by hand. That is the deep advantage: feature learning. Stacking layers with a non-linear activation is what gives the network this power; see Chapter 1.6.

The price is data and compute. A deep network has many weights, so it needs many examples and fast arithmetic. A small table with 200 rows will often do better with a simple model. A large image collection with millions of labelled photos can reward a deep model. Deep learning is not always better ML; it is a better fit when data and compute are plentiful.

The same nesting helps you read claims. AI-powered may mean a hand-written rule. Machine learning may mean a small regression. Deep learning says the model has many layers. Ask what data trained it and what task it solves.

figure.caption: The outer ring is AI, the middle is ML, the inner is DL. Notice that the DL examples also belong to ML and AI, while the chess engine belongs only to AI.

spec.aria: Three nested rings: artificial intelligence encloses machine learning, which encloses deep learning, with two example methods in each.

examples.question: Sort four systems into AI only, ML (not DL), or DL. Give one reason for each. Also give the count in each class and the total. (a) A chess program that follows rules written by a programmer. (b) Predicting a house price in rupees from its area using a straight-line fit on 200 past sales. (c) Recognising a face in a photo with a network of 8 layers. (d) Grouping 500 customers into 3 spend groups with no labels.
steps: Test (a): a chess program does a task that needs intelligence, but every rule is written by a person. No learning from data. Class: AI only.
Test (b): the program fits a straight line to 200 past sales. The rules come from data. One straight line is shallow, not many layers. Class: ML, not DL.
Test (c): the program is ML and has 8 layers that learn features from pixels. Class: DL.
Test (d): the program finds 3 groups from 500 customers with no labels. This is ML (unsupervised), and a shallow grouping method is not DL. Class: ML, not DL.
Count AI only: system (a) gives 1. Count ML not DL: systems (b) and (d) give 2. Count DL: system (c) gives 1. Total systems: 4.
examples.answer: AI only: 1 system; ML but not DL: 2 systems; DL: 1 system; total: 4 systems.
examples.check:
systems = [('a', 'AI only'), ('b', 'ML'), ('c', 'DL'), ('d', 'ML')]
ai_only = sum(1 for _, label in systems if label == 'AI only')
ml_not_dl = sum(1 for _, label in systems if label == 'ML')
dl = sum(1 for _, label in systems if label == 'DL')
total = len(systems)
print(ai_only)
print(ml_not_dl)
print(dl)
print(total)

traps: Calling any AI program machine learning. If every rule is typed in by a person, there is no learning from data.
Calling a single-layer model deep. Depth means many layers, not a large table of weights.
Assuming deep learning is always better. It needs more data and compute; a small dataset may favour a shallow model.
Mixing up the 1969 XOR limit with a limit of all neural networks. It is a limit of a single perceptron; multilayer networks can solve XOR.
Forgetting that unsupervised learning can be ML but not DL. k-means on 500 customers is ML; it has no deep layer stack.

quiz.q: Define AI, ML and DL in one line each.
quiz.a: AI: a machine does a task that needs intelligence. ML: the program improves from data instead of hand-written rules. DL: ML with many stacked layers that learn their own features.

quiz.q: Why is a hand-written chess engine AI but not ML?
quiz.a: It does a task that needs intelligence, so it is AI. Its move rules and search are written by a programmer; it does not improve its weights from data, so it is not ML.

quiz.q: A model uses 12 layers to classify crop disease from leaf photos. Is it AI, ML, DL? Explain.
quiz.a: It is AI, ML and DL. The task needs intelligence, so AI. It learns from labelled photos, so ML. It has 12 stacked layers and learns features from pixels, so DL.

quiz.q: A team has 300 labelled house sales and a table of 6 columns. Would you start with deep learning or a shallow model? Give two reasons.
quiz.a: Start with a shallow model. The dataset is small, so a model with many weights may overfit. The inputs are only 6 columns, so hand-designed features are easy and a deep feature learner has little to gain.
1943: McCulloch-Pitts neuron model. 1958: Rosenblatt's perceptron. 1969: XOR limit of a single perceptron. 1986: backpropagation revival for multilayer networks.

quiz.q: What did AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet result show in practical terms?
quiz.a: A deep CNN trained on a large labelled image dataset, with GPU compute, gave a large error drop. It showed that deep networks could beat hand-designed features on a hard vision task.

quiz.q: Sort: (i) expert system for train ticket rules, (ii) linear regression on past sales, (iii) 20-layer face network. Use the three tests.
quiz.a: (i) AI only: rules are hand-written, no data learning. (ii) ML, not DL: it learns from data but is shallow. (iii) DL: it is ML with 20 layers learning features.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the nesting helps in model choice: a fraud team may run a simple ML model on a few transaction columns, while a phone face unlock uses a deep network. Research now often starts from a pretrained large model and fine-tunes it, which is transfer learning at scale. Newer curricula add foundation models, model compression and deployment cost. Search next for representation learning, ImageNet, AlexNet, transformer scaling and foundation models.
